articles.title: Trump reportedly open to Iran sanctions relief for nuclear progress
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is reportedly open to giving economic sanctions relief and release frozen funds to Iran in exchange for concrete progress related to its nuclear program...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump is reportedly open to giving economic sanctions relief and release frozen funds to Iran in exchange for concrete progress related to its nuclear program, a U.S. official told American news outlets Axios and CNN on Monday.
Washington is engaging in "positive and constructive" talks via mediators, CNN quoted a U.S. official as saying, emphasizing that negotiators would not finalize an agreement unless nuclear-related concerns received full resolution.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request by Anadolu Agency (AA) for comment on the remarks.
The prospective diplomatic opening comes after Trump on Saturday rejected an Iranian proposal aimed at easing tensions and reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz, calling Tehran's conditions "unacceptable" amid the seven-month Iran war.
Trump said Sunday that he expects additional negotiations with Tehran this week, asserting that Iranian officials "overplayed" their hand during earlier talks.

articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has forcefully denied reports that his administration offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets in exchange for concessions on its nuclear program. The denial follows an investigative report detailing active backchannel negotiations between Washington and Tehran, highlighting the intense friction between clandestine diplomatic efforts and the public posturing required to manage domestic political narratives and regional alliances.
The mechanics of frozen assets and sanctions relief
The disputed report alleged that American negotiators proposed a framework wherein Iran would halt the advanced enrichment of uranium and cooperate with international inspectors in return for the unfreezing of billions of dollars in sovereign assets held in third-party jurisdictions. These funds, largely accumulated from oil sales prior to the reimposition of maximum pressure sanctions, are currently sequestered in financial institutions across Asia and the Middle East, subject to strict US Treasury waivers that limit their use to humanitarian goods.
Releasing these funds requires complex multilateral coordination. Any formal sanctions relief would necessitate navigating the "snapback" mechanism embedded in United Nations Security Council resolutions, a process that European allies have previously threatened to trigger if Iran's nuclear latency crosses specific thresholds. Consequently, backchannel discussions often focus on informal administrative waivers and the quiet non-enforcement of secondary sanctions on regional oil buyers, rather than the formal dismantling of the statutory sanctions architecture that the executive branch cannot easily reverse without congressional approval.
Domestic politics versus backchannel diplomacy
The President's swift and categorical rejection of the report underscores the severe domestic political liabilities associated with engaging Tehran. In the current political environment, any perceived concession to Iran is rapidly weaponized by opposition lawmakers and regional allies who view the Islamic Republic as the primary architect of Middle Eastern instability. By publicly declaring that no such offer was made, the administration attempts to insulate itself from accusations of appeasement, even as intelligence and diplomatic officials continue to explore avenues to prevent a nuclear breakout.

This dynamic creates a persistent paradox in US-Iran relations: the executive branch requires plausible deniability to conduct negotiations, yet the strategic signaling required to deter Iranian escalation often leaks to the press, forcing public denials that can simultaneously derail the very talks they are meant to conceal. Diplomatic veterans note that such public disavowals are standard operating procedure in high-stakes nuclear negotiations, where the mere acknowledgment of an offer can collapse the fragile domestic consensus required for the other side to accept it.
The legacy of the JCPOA and the snapback mechanism
The current diplomatic paralysis is inextricably linked to the collapse of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. Following the US withdrawal from the accord in 2018 and the subsequent reimposition of sweeping economic sanctions, Iran incrementally breached the treaty's limits on uranium enrichment and heavy water stockpiles. Today, the original framework is effectively defunct, leaving diplomats attempting to negotiate a "less for less" interim agreement that freezes Iran's most advanced nuclear activities in exchange for limited, phased access to its sequestered oil revenues.
Complicating these efforts is the looming threat of the UN snapback mechanism, a provision in Security Council Resolution 2231 that allows any participating state to unilaterally reimpose all pre-2015 international sanctions. European powers have repeatedly warned that Iran's refusal to cooperate with the International Atomic Energy Agency could trigger this mechanism, which would legally obligate even reluctant US allies to enforce a global embargo. This legal sword of Damocles serves as the primary leverage for Western negotiators, even as public political narratives demand a posture of maximum pressure rather than diplomatic compromise.
Constraints on Iran's nuclear program and regional fallout
Beyond the political optics, the substance of the alleged negotiations points to the narrowing window for a diplomatic solution. Iran's stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium has expanded significantly since the collapse of the 2015 nuclear accord, reducing the breakout time to a matter of weeks. Any credible agreement would require Tehran to physically dilute or export this stockpile, a concession that the Iranian supreme leadership has historically resisted without immediate, verifiable, and substantial economic relief.
- Enrichment Caps: Demands for Iran to dismantle advanced centrifuge cascades at the Natanz facility.
- Inspection Access: Restoring IAEA monitoring cameras and granting snap inspections of undeclared sites.
- Regional Proxy Restraint: Linking nuclear concessions to the curtailment of ballistic missile transfers to allied militias.
Regional actors, particularly Israel and the Gulf states, remain deeply skeptical of any bilateral arrangement between Washington and Tehran that lacks ironclad security guarantees. They argue that sanctions relief merely provides the Iranian state with the liquidity required to fund regional proxies and accelerate its conventional military programs. As the UN nuclear watchdog continues to report on Tehran's non-compliance, the gap between the public denials of diplomatic outreach and the urgent reality of the nuclear timeline continues to widen, leaving the region in a state of precarious, unmanaged escalation.

United States President Donald Trump on Tuesday strongly dismissed a report claiming that his administration was willing to grant sanctions relief and unfreeze assets for Iran in exchange for nuclear concessions. The clarification is significant as it challenges the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough in the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which is in its seventh month.
Trump Denies Offering Sanctions Relief
In a post on Truth Social, Trump called the reporting a “hoax” fueled by “Trump Derangement Syndrome.” Stating that he had not "offered them NOTHING”, Trump demanded that Axios withdraw the fake story immediately. “Axios just released a story that “Trump” offered Sanctions Relief and Frozen Funds to Iran. They should withdraw this fake story, IMMEDIATELY! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” he wrote.
The Axios report emerged amid the ongoing US-Iran war, which began following a joint US-Israeli strike on February 28 and an escalating global energy crisis driven by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The report, citing US officials, noted that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release Iranian frozen funds in return for “concrete Iranian steps regarding the nuclear programme.”

- President Trump is willing to provide Iran with sanctions relief and release frozen funds if Tehran makes progress on its nuclear program, but the offer comes with significant conditions.
President Donald Trump is willing to provide Iran with sanctions relief and release some frozen Iranian funds if Tehran makes concrete progress on its nuclear program, according to reports from CNN and Axios, as U.S. and Iranian officials pursue another diplomatic opening through mediators.
A U.S. official told CNN that Washington is engaged in "positive and constructive discussions through the mediators," but stressed that there will be no agreement unless Iran's nuclear issues are addressed.
The reported willingness to provide economic relief comes with significant conditions, however, and does not represent an unconditional offer to Tehran.
Trump himself denied the Axios report, saying he'd offered Iran nothing. He called for the news organization to withdraw the story.
The reports of any potential movement followed Trump's rejection Saturday of Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in exchange for the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and other economic concessions.
Trump said Sunday he expected additional talks with Iran this week but said Tehran's latest proposal was unacceptable.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Trump said, according to CNN. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand."
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Sunday that Iran had sought sanctions relief and access to billions of dollars in frozen assets before making the nuclear commitments Washington is demanding.
"The bottom line is they were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk," Waltz told CNN's Jake Tapper on "State of the Union."
The Associated Press reported Monday that mediators are continuing to work toward a U.S.-Iran agreement despite Trump's rejection of Tehran's latest proposal.
Four officials familiar with the discussions said behind-the-scenes efforts were continuing to broker an agreement aimed at ending the fighting and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has indicated it is flexible on the nuclear question. The two sides remain divided over timing and which side would make the first move, according to the officials.
Reuters separately reported Monday that Qatari mediators were expected to hold talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in New York and separately with U.S. officials Monday or Tuesday.
The report said the discussions were expected to focus on an amended version of Iran's seven-day proposal presented last week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
Iran's latest proposal calls for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear discussions in exchange for the lifting of the U.S. blockade and economic penalties, according to the AP.
Two regional officials said mediators are working on a proposal under which the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and the U.S. blockade would be lifted before additional sanctions are removed.
One regional official said the United States is seeking Iranian concessions that could include allowing international inspectors into the country.
The diplomatic effort comes after an earlier memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran collapsed within days of being reached in June. The agreement envisioned discussions of Iran's nuclear program over a 60-day period.
U.S. officials remain skeptical of Iranian assurances, particularly after Iran fired on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest talks also come as the conflict enters its eighth month and continues to disrupt international energy markets.
AP reported Monday that Brent crude was trading above $108 a barrel as fighting and uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz continued to affect global oil supplies.
Trump has repeatedly said preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon is a central condition of any agreement.
"The key is Iran will not have a nuclear weapon," Trump said Monday.
The latest diplomatic push leaves the United States and Iran engaged through intermediaries even as they remain divided over the terms, timing and sequencing of any potential agreement.

For Iran, the tightening US economic blockade on commercial aviation and shipping has generated severe internal financial stress, forcing a retreat on its nuclear enrichment red lines.

articles.title: How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom will provide Saudi Arabia with military support in its escalating war against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group, the British government said this week.
The UK agreed to provide air-to-air refuelling of Saudi fighter jets that are conducting missions after the kingdom requested air-defence support, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday.

However, it will not directly join Riyadh’s renewed conflict with the Houthis, which began in 2014 after the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa along with large areas of northwest Yemen, driving the internationally recognised government to Aden. The two sides had reached a United Nations-mediated ceasefire in 2022, before fighting broke out again this year amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Particularly heavy fighting erupted again two weeks ago as the Houthis advanced against Yemeni forces to the Red Sea coast, taking the strategic port city of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandeb, the entry point for shipping entering the Red Sea from the south.
Since then, the group has targeted Riyadh as well as Saudi oil infrastructure, including taking out a section of the vital East-West Pipeline that had allowed Saudi to make oil exports despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz triggered by the Iran war.
Before the latest bout of fighting broke out, the Houthis had also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Red Sea, through which about 12 percent of global trade passes.
Here is what you need to know about what support the UK will provide:
What has the UK announced?
British PM Burnham said London had accepted a Saudi request for what he called “defensive air-to-air refuelling”. Britain will deploy one Royal Air Force Voyager tanker aircraft to assist with this in the coming days.
“We have received a request from the kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support,” Burnham told reporters on his way to the UN General Assembly in New York this week, adding that he had agreed to the request on the advice of his defence and foreign secretaries.
Burnham said the arrangement would be “time-limited” and would be kept under review. However, the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) has not specified a timetable.
Burnham said the UK was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region”, linking the need to keep oil export routes open.
In a statement, the MoD told Al Jazeera that the decision to provide support “builds on the UK’s existing military contribution to Saudi Arabia’s air defence”, including the deployment of “air defence equipment and UK personnel helping to protect against missile and drone attacks”.
“Saudi Arabia and Yemen are long-standing partners of the United Kingdom, and play a vital role in regional stability. It is in the UK’s interest to protect regional stability, protecting vital trade and energy supplies and encouraging a diplomatic resolution to the conflict in Yemen,” the MoD said.
What is air-to-air refuelling?
Air-to-air refuelling is the transfer of aviation fuel from one aircraft to another in mid-air.
Refuelling in mid-air will allow Saudi fighter jets to remain airborne past their fuel limits, in order to spend more time patrolling Saudi airspace or responding to incoming threats.
Saudi Arabia faces potential threats to cities, military installations and energy infrastructure spread across a very large area.
While the Houthis have largely targeted Saudi cities in the south of the country, close to the Yemeni border, they have hit targets in the capital city, Riyadh, in the country’s centre.
During Israel’s war on Gaza, the Houthis also launched missiles towards Israel.
What’s the UK-Saudi Arabia military relationship?
Britain has particularly deep military ties with Saudi Arabia, one of the biggest buyers of British military equipment, stretching back for decades.
Under the Conservative Party government of John Major in the 1990s, and the later Labour governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown from the late 1990s to 2010, the UK supplied Tornado and Hawk aircraft and other equipment to the kingdom, involving the UK defence company BAE Systems.
The relationship was expanded to include Eurofighter Typhoon combat aircraft. In 2006, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy 72 Typhoons in a deal worth $40bn that also included technology transfer and training.
London has also provided defensive assistance during the ongoing regional conflict. Earlier this year, the UK deployed its Sky Sabre air-defence system to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom from Iranian missile attacks on United States military assets and other infrastructure on Saudi territory.
Will this make a difference?
The air refuelling assistance from London could improve Saudi Arabia’s ability to defend itself to some degree, but what the UK has announced so far is limited, experts say.
The UK’s support carries more political weight than military significance, according to Chris Doyle, director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding.
“In military terms this is not a major change-up,” Doyle said, arguing that what matters more for Saudi Arabia right now is having visible international backing as it confronts the Houthis.
Riyadh will be keen to avoid appearing “isolated” in the conflict, particularly as other countries remain reluctant to become directly involved, he said. Most significantly, the administration of US President Donald Trump has already indicated it will not involve itself in the Saudi-Houthi fighting or against Houthi blockades on Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea.
Trump said the Houthis had assured US officials that they had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea.
As for other states, “Many are reluctant to get involved. They see this as being part of the wider US-Iran conflict, and they just are hesitant,” Doyle said.

articles.title: Crude Oil Futures Jump About 3% as Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Reignite Supply Concerns - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: Crude Oil Futures Jump About 3% as Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Reignite Supply Concerns  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
Crude oil futures climbed approximately 3% on September 24 U.S. time, reaching their highest level in a week. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militant group launched missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia's oil-related facilities and its capital, intensifying concerns over Middle East supply disruptions.
Settlement prices showed Brent crude futures up $3.52 (3.4%) at $106.60 per barrel (approximately ¥17,000), while U.S. WTI futures rose $2.45 (2.7%) to $94.61 per barrel (approximately ¥15,000). Both contracts recorded gains of roughly 5% at intraday highs. September gains have reached over 17% for Brent and over 10% for WTI.
However, trading remained volatile throughout the session. Reports that the United States and Iran were in discussions over reopening the Strait of Hormuz eased supply crunch fears, pushing prices back from their highs.
The Houthis announced on September 24 that they had carried out missile and drone attacks on "important targets" in the Saudi capital Riyadh and on facilities belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in the Red Sea coastal city of Yanbu.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition confirmed the same day that it had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis, thwarting attacks on the southern city of Taif and the Red Sea coastal area of Yanbu.
Supply risks and geopolitical factors intersect
The latest attack underscores that the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, remains exposed to geopolitical risk. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted oil facilities and airports within Saudi Arabia, and in 2019 an attack on the Abqaiq crude processing facility temporarily halted roughly half of the country's production capacity.
That said, the Yanbu attack largely compounds damage already inflicted on the export network. Saudi exports have plummeted since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran in late February. According to vessel tracking data, Saudi crude loadings have fallen by more than 70%, from over 7.5 million barrels per day in January-February to approximately 2.3 million barrels per day in August and around 2.1 million barrels per day in the first half of September.

The East-West Pipeline, Saudi Arabia's only bypass route around the strait, also halted operations after a drone attack on September 10 damaged three pumping stations. While operations resumed at reduced rates this week, satellite imagery and vessel data indicate that crude loading onto ships from the port of Yanbu had still not resumed as of September 24, with full restoration expected to take more than six weeks. The pipeline carries approximately 4 million barrels per day of crude to the Red Sea side, equivalent to about 4% of global supply.

Market focus is on whether the attack on Yanbu on the Red Sea coast leads to direct supply disruptions. Yanbu hosts a major oil export terminal and refinery, and if these facilities become inoperable, Red Sea export routes could be affected.
Speculation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz
A factor that capped price gains was the report that the United States and Iran are discussing reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The strait is a critical chokepoint through which roughly 20% of global crude shipments pass, and markets have reacted nervously each time Iran has hinted at potential closure.
The discussions reportedly involve a phased deal in which Iran would allow navigation through the strait in exchange for the United States lifting its naval blockade and economic sanctions on Iran, as well as granting access to frozen assets. According to Reuters, the two countries had reached a memorandum of understanding on the same framework on June 17, but it collapsed after hostilities resumed. The U.S. military has been escorting tankers through the strait, but Iranian attacks on commercial vessels continue, and Gulf states have refused to pay the transit fees Iran has demanded.
The prospects for an agreement remain uncertain. President Trump has indicated a deal could be reached after the November 3 midterm elections, while former U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross puts the probability of a pre-election agreement at 30%. Ross noted that both sides actually have stronger incentives to reach a deal before the election.
While details and progress of the negotiations remain unclear, any de-escalation would significantly reduce Middle East supply risks. Investor attention is now focused on the tug-of-war between two opposing factors: the persistence of Houthi attacks and the trajectory of U.S.-Iran talks.
Ripple effects on Asian buyers
The supply chain disruption is directly impacting Asia, the primary buyer of Saudi crude. Export destinations are dominated by Asian countries: China accounts for 22%, South Korea 14%, Japan 13%, India 10%, and the United States 5%. Moreover, at the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, the Houthis seized key positions in September and declared a blockade. Vessels heading to Asia from the Red Sea side must now travel north through the Suez Canal, pass the Strait of Gibraltar, and round the Cape of Good Hope—a voyage of approximately 13,140 nautical miles, adding nearly a month of travel time compared to the roughly 3,370 nautical miles (about 10 days) via the Strait of Hormuz.
According to preliminary petroleum statistics from Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), Japan's Middle East dependence for crude oil imports fell to 58.9% in July 2026, down 28.7 percentage points from the same month a year earlier. This marks the tenth consecutive month of year-on-year declines, with dependence dropping from 95.1% in January to nearly two-thirds of that level within six months. In July, the United States was the top import source at 4.34 million kiloliters (4.6 times the year-earlier level), followed by the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Japan has clearly been shifting procurement toward routes that do not pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

Japan also has reserve capacity. Combined public and private oil reserves stand at approximately 200 days' worth (of which private reserves account for roughly 95 days). METI Minister Ryosei Akazawa stated on September 15 that tankers for October procurement have already departed for Japan, indicating that additional reserve releases are unnecessary. The government will assess the recovery situation on the Saudi side before deciding whether releases are needed from November onward.
By contrast, U.S. reserves are running thin. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) stood at 284.6 million barrels as of September 18—the lowest level since 1982.
Among market participants, some view geopolitical premiums as supporting crude prices in the short term, while others note that concerns over a global economic slowdown are weighing on demand forecasts, capping upside potential.

articles.title: Oil at $100 Again: What the Iran Talks, the Houthis and a Saudi Pipeline Mean for Prices - Latin Times
articles.summary: Oil at $100 Again: What the Iran Talks, the Houthis and a Saudi Pipeline Mean for Prices  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Brent, the global crude benchmark, traded at roughly $100.30 a barrel on Wednesday afternoon. The price has been circling that level for weeks. On September 10, Brent jumped above $107, its strongest showing in nearly four months. It then settled at $100.34 on Monday and finished Tuesday slightly lower, near $99.25.
A War, Not Ordinary Market Swings, Is Setting the Price
The current run began when the United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28. Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz nearly stopped, and the International Energy Agency has described the result as the "largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." Brent came within a whisker of $120 in the first weeks of the war.
The picture has improved since then, though not fully. A commodity strategist at TD Securities estimates that Middle East flows have climbed to about 80% of their prewar pace, while JPMorgan analysts calculated that total shipments were still about 6 million barrels a day under the 2025 average, CNBC reported.
Houthis Turn the Red Sea Into a Second Front
Yemen is the other pressure point. Houthi fighters have reportedly seized Perim Island after capturing the port of Mokha, and they declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia in July. Attacks on vessels near Bab al-Mandeb have pushed the kingdom to send crude through the Suez Canal or around Africa to reach Asian customers, The National reported.
Washington has held back for now. President Donald Trump has decided against striking the Houthis despite Saudi requests, according to officials cited by The New York Times.
Riyadh's main detour around Hormuz was knocked out first. The East-West pipeline, built to move 7 million barrels a day to the Red Sea, was shut on September 11 after what the Saudi Energy Ministry called multiple attacks. Reuters sources said it resumed on Tuesday at a lower rate.
Full recovery is not here yet. Wire reporting describes the restart as being in its early stages, with export volumes targeted for later this week and Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure still continuing.
Talks in New York Take the Edge Off Prices
US and Iranian negotiators are meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Trump said on Tuesday that people he spoke with saw strong momentum toward an agreement, though he has also indicated that a final deal could wait until after the midterm elections.
Analysts see limited room to fall. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com argued that a believable Hormuz reopening plus stronger Saudi exports could drag Brent toward the low $90s, but that further declines would get harder unless physical flows improve. Salih Yilmaz of Bloomberg Intelligence said Brent could stay under $100 if current trends hold, while warning that inventories and other buffers are thinner than earlier in the conflict.
Why the Fed Is Watching Every Barrel
Expensive crude is now feeding into interest-rate policy. On September 16, the Federal Reserve lifted its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 3.75%–4%, its first increase in more than three years, in a unanimous 12–0 vote. Policymakers pointed to inflation driven partly by the oil spike, and a strong majority of them expect another hike before year-end.
For fuel-importing countries and households, that means costlier gasoline and costlier borrowing at the same time.
The outlook rests on three questions: whether the New York talks deliver a Hormuz arrangement, how quickly Saudi pipeline volumes recover, and whether the Houthi–Saudi confrontation spreads across Bab al-Mandeb. A collapse in negotiations or fresh attacks on tankers could send prices up fast.
Goldman Sachs has mapped the range. Its base case has Brent at $85 in December, but the bank says prices could top $120 if Gulf output averages 4 million barrels a day below prewar levels through 2027, versus a 0.5 million barrel shortfall in its central scenario.

President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting reports that he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds for concrete steps on its nuclear program.
"This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday.
Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified U.S. officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue.
Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbors and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic nuclear energy capacity.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation," said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks," Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons."
U.S. and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators Monday as part of a renewed effort to end the seven-month war, according to officials of both countries.
Iran insisted Sunday that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Araghchi told reporters at the U.N. Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians' push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Araghchi said mediators facilitating Tehran's talks with Washington had not officially relayed a U.S. rejection.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi posted.
The war, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February as "Operation Epic Fury," has killed thousands of people, severely disrupted global energy supplies, pushing up oil prices and fueling global inflation.
Iran and its allies have responded by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck U.S. allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles, while its Houthi allies in Yemen have hit Saudi interests.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Houthi rebeles have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Oil prices rose for a second successive session on Tuesday as lingering concern over Middle East supply outweighed signs of recovering crude exports from the region.
Brent crude futures had risen $1.49, or 1.4%, to $106.77 a barrel by 0326 GMT while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was at $93.94, up $1.34, or 1.5%. Both benchmarks closed the previous session at nearly $1 a barrel higher.

Red Sea crisis: What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?
A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets.
The group, which has controlled much of northern Yemen for over a decade, has seized fresh territory from the pro-government forces and threatened shipping traffic, notably that of Saudi Arabia, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the maritime chokepoint linking the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".
But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.
Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.
The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.
While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.
Who are the Houthis and what’s going on in Yemen?
Officially called Ansar Allah (“helpers of God”), the Houthis were founded in 1994 by cleric Hussein al-Houthi. Rooted in Zaydi Shiaism, they want more autonomy for northern Yemen, where much of the country’s population is concentrated.
Led by Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the brother of Hussein, the group fought a series of wars against the government of Ali Abdullah Saleh in the 2000s. Their slogan is “God is the greatest, death to America, death to Israel, curse the Jews, victory to Islam".
The Houthis seized much of Yemen’s northwest, including the capital, Sanaa, between 2014 and 2016 at the height of the Yemeni civil war, principally fought between the Houthis and pro-government forces backed by a Saudi-led international coalition. Since then it has expanded its fighting force from 30,000 in 2015 to an estimated 350,000 by 2024, although counts vary.
Since 2023, the Houthis have also attacked over 100 commercial ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, principally targeting those linked to Israel amid the country’s genocide in Gaza as well as from Saudi Arabia.
In 2022, the UN brokered an informal ceasefire, which left the Houthis with around 30 percent of the country containing 80 percent of the population, albeit under an ongoing Saudi-led blockade.
This period of relative calm collapsed in July after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport. The Houthis declared a maritime blockade and attacked vessels, mainly Saudi, in the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea for the first time in months.
Training and tactics
While the Houthis are independent of Iran, the Islamic Republic has courted the group as a regional partner since at least the late 2000s.
Much of that support was overseen by Qasem Soleimani, leader of Quds Force, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps’ elite overseas wing, until his assassination by the US in January 2020.
The Houthis have also collaborated with other members of the Axis, including Hezbollah, which has met with Houthi leaders in Iraq and Syria, according to UN experts.
Russia has also forged ties with the Houthis since the civil war began, providing it with targeting data and deploying military intelligence officers to Yemen, as Middle East Eye revealed in August 2024.
Moscow’s support has been less than it afforded Syrian President Bashar al-Assad during the Syrian civil war, but it has still used its UN Security Council veto to stall arms embargoes targeting the group.
The Houthis have also used open-source intelligence, including shipping traffic data from maritime intelligence websites, to locate and attack vessels in the Red Sea.
In September, Anthropic suggested the group had used its Claude AI model to develop missile navigation systems.
Medium-range missiles
There are no indications that the Houthis have access to long-range missiles, including intercontinental ballistic missiles, making attacks outside the Middle East and Africa unlikely.
But their medium-range missile capability is such that they have hit targets in northern Israel, around 2,000km from Sanaa, including Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport.
Fabian Hinz, senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research (CAR).
“Tehran has managed to secure a seemingly steady flow of technology to the Houthis and has proven willing to share even some of its most advanced capabilities, such as the Kheibar Shekan.”
The Houthis’ armoury includes the Palestine-2 precision-guided series, first promoted by the group in 2024, which they say has a range of 2,150km and uses solid fuel, meaning it can be deployed quickly.
The movement also claims the Palestine-2 system is hypersonic and can carry a 500kg warhead, allowing it to manoeuvre while travelling at Mach 5 (more than 6,000 km/h), making it harder to intercept.
But analysts have cast doubt on this, pointing out that only Russia, China, India and the US have hypersonic missiles, and that none of these can fly as fast as the speeds claimed by the Houthis.
The Houthis have also released footage of other medium-range ballistic missiles, including the Hatem-2, which appears to be a variant of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan (“castle-breaker”) system. It has a range of 1,450km, can carry a 500kg warhead, and is among the Islamic Republic’s most advanced systems.
But the scale of the Houthi missile arsenal is unclear, given that its weapons are developed and trafficked covertly.
“They could have one missile or they could have one hundred,” says Wolf-Christian Paes, a global security consultant and senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
“We really know next to nothing about the numbers of each missile system that they have, until they fire them.”
Short-range ballistic and anti-ship cruise missiles
This, analysts suggest, was an unorthodox strategy, given that ballistic missiles follow a parabolic curve and can easily miss a moving target, indicating that the group was running low on other, better-suited armaments.
Since then, the Houthis have also used anti-ship cruise missiles, which skim the surface of the water and are more accurate.

Many of these weapons closely match Iranian technology and require complex production facilities that have not been identified in Yemen. Analysts told Middle East Eye that the parts may have been supplied by Tehran and then assembled locally.
“In some cases, the Houthis are even receiving missiles in ready-made kits with assembly instructions,” says Rob Hunter-Perkins, head of research at CAR.
Hinz says that the Houthis also inherited older missile models from the Yemeni government when the group captured Sanaa in 2014 and modified some of these systems, albeit “likely with foreign assistance”.
These include ageing Soviet-era air-to-air missiles, which the Houthis converted into surface-to-air missiles, and Soviet-built surface-to-air missiles, retrofitted into anti-ship ballistic missiles.
But Hinz says that “it is unclear, however, how much of the Houthi arsenal of these legacy systems remains”.
Drones
But as the civil war progressed, the Saudi-led coalition gained control of the skies and destroyed many of these vehicles, with the group increasingly turning to drones during ground offensives.
Some drones, including the Jaffa and Samad models, can travel over 2,000km and have been used to target Israel, although few have been able to evade Israel’s aerial defence systems, including Iron Dome.
Parts of these systems are most likely imported from Iran. But development and assembly may sometimes take place domestically, Hinz says, pointing to recent evidence that the Houthis are developing hydrogen-powered drones, capable of carrying larger payloads for longer distances.
Paes says that ships are less vulnerable to drone attacks, and so serve as "more of a political weapon".
“Shipping companies are risk-averse, so drones are a low-cost way for the Houthis to tell ship owners: ‘I can get to you’, even if they are not an effective way to sink the ship or do real damage.”
Guns and small arms
Owning a Kalashnikov or handgun is a rite of passage for many Yemeni men, and carrying guns in public is largely unrestricted in Houthi-controlled areas.
Others have circulated in Yemen for decades, with many weapons seized by the Houthis during the height of the Yemen War.
These include powerful German-made G3 rifles, which can fire up to 600 rounds per minute and have a range of up to 800 metres with sights.

articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan traveled to Washington on Monday to meet with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The talks come as Houthi attacks intensify, increasing pressure on Riyadh.
Riyadh is seeking broader security support from the United States. Attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis are also threatening shipping in the Red Sea.
Riyadh seeks military support from the US
Saudi Arabia has asked Washington for military assistance against the Houthis. According to information published by Reuters citing sources, the United States has so far refused to strike the Houthis but has agreed to provide Riyadh with intelligence and assistance in identifying targets.
The kingdom itself has faced missile and drone attacks by the Houthis. Two ballistic missiles and two drones were reportedly intercepted near Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis, however, distinguish between Saudi and US targets. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior group representative, told the Associated Press on Sept. 20 that the Houthis did not intend to attack US vessels in the Red Sea. At the same time, he urged countries not to support Saudi Arabia.
US President Donald Trump has also said the Houthis assured Washington that American shipping would not be targeted. This situation is leaving Saudi Arabia exposed to more direct military pressure while it seeks greater support from the United States.
Red Sea crisis could raise global costs
The Red Sea provides access to the Suez Canal, one of the world’s most important trade routes. About 26,000 vessels passed through the canal in 2023. By volume, the route accounts for roughly 10% of global maritime trade and 22% of container shipping.
Finished products, consumer goods, machinery and equipment, components, energy products and other cargoes are transported along the route between Asia, Europe, the Mediterranean and the US East Coast.
Disruptions to shipping could increase freight, insurance and fuel costs for US companies. Vessels are being forced to use alternative, longer routes.
By mid-2024, the tonnage of vessels passing through the Suez Canal had fallen by about 70%. During the same period, vessel traffic around the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa rose by 89%. According to the UN Conference on Trade and Development, route diversions increased global demand for shipping capacity by 3% and demand for container ships by 12%.
Saudi oil route also under pressure
Another major risk for Saudi Arabia is the threat to its oil infrastructure. The 1,200-kilometer East-West oil pipeline transports crude from fields in the country’s east to the Red Sea, allowing Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Reuters, the pipeline carried about 4 million to 5 million barrels of oil per day in recent months. This volume represents roughly 4% to 5% of global oil supplies.
Operations on the pipeline were temporarily suspended after a drone attack on Sept. 13, forcing Saudi Arabia to direct more oil to terminals on the Gulf coast.
On Sept. 20, Saudi Aramco loaded about 14 million barrels of crude onto seven large tankers at the Ras Tanura port. The volume of Saudi oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz also rose to 2.9 million barrels per day from about 700,000 barrels per day in August.
Washington faces a difficult choice
Against this backdrop, the meeting between Faisal bin Farhan and Marco Rubio carries significance beyond bilateral relations. Washington must support an ally whose oil infrastructure and shipping routes are under pressure while also taking into account signals from the Houthis that they intend to keep US vessels out of the confrontation.
The central question for the United States is how much support to provide for Saudi Arabia’s security without becoming drawn into a broader military presence in Yemen. Riyadh wants stronger defenses, while the Houthis seek to avoid direct confrontation with the United States and continue pressuring Saudi Arabia.
A prolonged disruption of the Red Sea route could affect shipping costs, energy markets and, ultimately, the prices paid by companies and consumers worldwide.

Trump denies offering concessions as Iran pushes Hormuz plan, flight disruption persists
The US-Iran war remains caught between diplomacy and confrontation, with President Donald Trump denying that Washington has offered Tehran concessions even as mediators continue efforts to end seven months of fighting.
Iran says it remains ready for negotiations and is awaiting a US response to proposals aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, oil prices fell on Tuesday as crude exports from the Middle East showed signs of recovery.
For UAE residents, the main developments this Tuesday afternoon and evening are the continuing diplomatic push, uncertainty over Hormuz, easing oil prices and continuing changes to regional and international flight schedules.
Here is what you need to know on September 29.
Trump has rejected reports that Washington offered Iran sanctions relief or the release of frozen funds in return for concessions over Tehran’s nuclear programme.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING,” Trump said in a social media post.
The comments follow Trump’s rejection of Iran’s proposed seven-day plan, which envisaged a pause in regional fighting, the lifting of the US blockade on Iranian ports and sanctions relief before reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Despite rejecting the proposal, Trump has indicated that he expects negotiations to continue.
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday in another attempt to find a path towards ending the war.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who remained in New York following the UN General Assembly, said Tehran was waiting for Washington’s response to its proposals.
Further negotiations are expected to focus on an amended version of Iran’s seven-day plan.
Iran says reopening Hormuz remains conditional on meeting its demands and insists diplomacy is the only way to resolve the conflict.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has also said Tehran is prepared to discuss its nuclear programme and other issues but will not accept what he described as coercion.
Significant differences therefore remain, despite both sides keeping diplomatic channels open.
Saudi Arabia and the United States have stressed the importance of maritime security as fighting in Yemen and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz continue to threaten regional trade.
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed developments in Yemen as well as security and freedom of navigation through Hormuz and Bab Al Mandab during talks in Washington.
Saudi Arabia has called for unrestricted navigation through international waterways and for conditions in the Strait of Hormuz to return to those that existed before the war began on February 28.
The talks come amid continuing concern over Houthi attacks and their impact on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping.
Washington is also increasing financial pressure on Iran’s regional networks.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Finance Minister Yassine Jaber in Washington and urged Beirut to take steps to disrupt Iranian and Hezbollah financial networks.
Bessent also pressed Lebanon to advance reforms to restore confidence in its banking system.
The move adds a financial dimension to US efforts to restrict Iran’s influence across the region while diplomatic efforts continue over the wider conflict.
Oil prices fell on Tuesday as investors focused on signs that more crude is leaving the Middle East despite ongoing disruption from the war.
Brent crude fell nearly 2 per cent to around $103.32 a barrel during afternoon trading, while US West Texas Intermediate fell to around $90.65.
Saudi Arabia has resumed oil loadings from its Red Sea port of Yanbu after restarting the East-West Pipeline.
Preliminary data also showed crude exports from major Middle Eastern producers rising to around 12.8 million barrels per day in September, their highest level since February.
However, some of the increase still depends on more costly shipping workarounds, while uncertainty around Hormuz keeps oil prices elevated.
Iraqi Airways is preparing to restart flights to Iran in October after Iraq secured a special exemption from US sanctions.
Iraq suspended flights to and from Iran last week after Washington restricted services involving Iranian airlines.
The exemption will initially allow Iraqi Airways to operate services between Iran and the Shiite holy city of Najaf once it completes regulatory and technical requirements.
The arrangement is expected to run for one month initially.
UAE travellers continue to face select delays and cancellations as regional tensions keep airline schedules fluid.
The latest Gulf News flight tracker shows individual Emirates, flydubai and other services affected, while airlines continue to advise passengers to confirm their flight status before travelling to the airport.
Air Canada has extended the suspension of its Dubai services until the end of March 2027, citing the situation in the Middle East.
The wider UAE aviation network continues to operate, and not every delay or cancellation is related to the regional conflict.
Passengers should check directly with their airline for the latest flight status.
The immediate focus remains on whether mediators can narrow the substantial differences between Washington and Tehran.
Iran is waiting for a US response to its latest proposals, but Trump’s insistence that he has offered Tehran no concessions underlines how far apart the two sides remain.
The Strait of Hormuz remains central to any settlement. A sustained increase in shipping through the waterway would ease pressure on global energy markets, while further disruption could quickly reverse Tuesday’s fall in oil prices.
For UAE travellers, airline schedules remain subject to change, making direct checks with carriers particularly important before departure.

articles.title: Multiple trade routes help Iran evade sanctions - GIS Reports
articles.summary: Multiple trade routes help Iran evade sanctions  GIS Reports
articles.full_text:
Tehran’s economy is battered, yet parallel trade networks prevent its complete economic isolation.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
- With Gulf access restricted, Iran uses costlier northern and eastern corridors
- Russia, China, Pakistan provide alternatives to Western-controlled routes
- Sanctions hurt Iran without delivering Washington’s desired outcome
- For comprehensive insights, tune into our AI-powered podcast here
To break the stalemate in its war with Iran, the administration of United States President Donald Trump is now trying to make Iran an international economic outcast with a new regime of sanctions. Iran has survived economic, military and diplomatic pressure from the U.S. and its allies since the 1979 Iranian revolution, albeit at great cost to its people.
This time, too, the Iranians expect to evade the most devastating impact of U.S. sanctions through the transportation and logistics networks they have created over the years to deal with Western pressure. Iran’s key partners in this effort so far have been Russia, Pakistan and China. This time around, Iran might also look to Turkiye as both a market and supplier, while expecting lukewarm implementation of sanctions or requests for exemptions from India.
The current war with Iran started because President Trump believed that his “maximum pressure” campaign against Iran was proving inadequate in preventing Tehran from developing nuclear weapons, neutralizing Iranian-backed terror networks and stopping the country’s missile armament.
The “Economic D-Day” announced by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August 2026 is an enhanced version of the February 2025 authorization the U.S. Treasury had to “impose maximum economic pressure” on the Iranian government.
Tehran circumventing sanctions
Before February 2025, Iran’s total trade stood at $110 billion annually. The sanctions limited Iran’s ability to sell its oil and to import commodities, yet China, Iraq and Turkiye remained Iran’s largest trading partners. Over the following year, China purchased 80-90 percent of Iran’s crude oil, worth nearly $32 billion. Trade with Iraq and Turkiye, both of which share land borders with Iran, was $10 billion and $5 billion, respectively.
The war that began on February 28, 2026, has disrupted Iran’s economy significantly, but there is no evidence that it has been completely crippled. Iran’s neighbors continue to serve as a lifeline, with cross-border commerce continuing in various forms, including illicit exchanges tolerated by border officials.
Among countries in Iran’s immediate neighborhood, the United Arab Emirates is the only one that has demonstrated the will to confront Iran, especially in the aftermath of Iran’s missile and drone attacks. Historically, the UAE was Iran’s second-largest trading partner, totaling $28 billion in 2024, for example. But the UAE implemented the U.S. “maximum pressure” sanctions and more recently, on August 19, 2026, suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran.
This meant that Iran lost all residual economic advantages of its historical business ties with the UAE, especially Dubai, where Iranian traders were once ubiquitous.
Limited by war and sanctions, Iran’s clerical regime, increasingly under control of the militant Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), understands that it can no longer depend on its Gulf ports as the main venue for its imports and exports. Tehran is now increasingly using its Caspian ports, including Bandar Anzali and Amirabad, and its land borders to manage continued economic activity.
Iran’s alternative trade routes
The Caspian corridor, free of disruption from the U.S. navy, allows Iran to maintain supplies of wheat, corn and edible oil, as well as military materials. But the Caspian ports have limited capacity and can only handle smaller vessels. Additionally, in July 2026, Ukraine targeted Iran-linked vessels in the Caspian Sea.
Using trucks to move goods through northern land routes is also much more expensive than shipping goods through ocean links. But in its effort to survive, Iran appears willing to pay that price for now; shipments across the Caspian Sea have reportedly increased significantly.
Iran-Pakistan trade and transport links
Iran and Pakistan share a relatively porous 900-kilometer border straddled by the ethnic Baloch people. Pakistan’s mediation role in the Iran war seems to have provided a boost to their trade and transport ties, which has, in turn, helped Iran evade Western sanctions.
Even before the latest war, Iran and Pakistan had tried to expand their economic and commercial partnership, in keeping with Pakistani leaders’ decades-old goal of regional economic integration with neighboring Muslim countries. Following President Trump implementing his maximum pressure sanctions, first in 2018 and reintroducing them in early 2025, Iran and Pakistan signed 12 agreements in August 2025, setting a target of $10 billion in bilateral trade by 2028.
Iranian-Pakistani commerce in March 2025 alone reached $3.13 billion. In its effort to circumvent sanctions, even this relatively small volume of trade was important for Iran, especially because cash payments and barter arrangements helped it bypass dollar-clearing requirements. Soon after mediating a ceasefire between Iran and the U.S. in June, Pakistan allowed the entry of goods originating from third countries into Iran overland through Pakistan.
When Iran attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, Pakistan designated six road corridors linking its ports in Karachi, including Port Qasim, as well as in Gwadar, to the Gabd and Taftan land crossings through Balochistan for trade with Iran. These crossings have enabled exchanges in daily essentials as well as fuel, including electricity and gas.
The economy along the Iran-Pakistan land border operates with both formal customs procedures and smuggling of a wide range of goods, including liquified petroleum gas and other petroleum products, steel, food, agricultural goods and some manufactured items. Pakistan benefits by receiving cheap Iranian fuel and consumer goods, while Iranian suppliers are able to access Pakistan’s market and hard-currency transaction mechanisms.
Iran and Pakistan are currently implementing a barter mechanism and have applied the Customs Convention on the International Transport of Goods under Cover of TIR Carnets (TIR Convention, 1975), both of which enable them to bypass sanctions by avoiding the scrutiny in traditional banking channels. Pakistan often grants temporary exemptions from normal banking-instrument requirements for essential exports to Iran.
Iranians and Pakistanis seem to believe that the development of these overland routes has a long-term significance that will outlast the current war.
Husain Haqqani
Pakistan has also eased some export rules to facilitate transit trade between Iran and Central Asian countries through its territory. Islamabad has temporarily waived formal banking rules for essential supplies to Iran as well as Pakistani exports to Central Asian states, trying to bolster its own exports. As a consequence, Iran is building resilient transportation corridors through Pakistan and into Central Asia.
All of this ties in with Pakistan’s geostrategic ambitions. Islamabad has, for years, sought to make Pakistan a transit trade and energy corridor between the Middle East and Central Asia. Its leaders see an opportunity to attain that goal while the U.S. tries to bring the Iranian regime to heel through economic measures.
Iranians and Pakistanis seem to believe that the development of these overland routes has a long-term significance that will outlast the current war.
Iran and Russia
As two countries that are revisionist, revolutionary and seek to reprise their pride and status, Iran and Russia have a lot in common. Both Iran and Russia face Western sanctions and have built interdependence in financial, commercial and transportation fields.
Over time, Iran and Russia have moved to conduct bilateral financial settlements using a rial-ruble exchange bypassing the SWIFT architecture. Currently, 90 percent of their bilateral trade is through this mechanism linking Iran’s homegrown interbank telecommunication and financial messaging system SEPAM to Russia’s alternative to SWIFT, called SPFS. Even though bilateral trade stands at only $5 billion, it avoids Western sanctions and banking restrictions.
Given its geography, regional influence and strategic interests, Russia has been key to Iran’s attempts to build resilient and efficient supply chains. The 2025 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty between the two countries institutionalized what has been built over the previous two decades.
The central element of this effort is the International North-South Transit Corridor (INSTC), which was established in 2000 by India, Russia and Iran as an alternative transportation corridor and trade route to the Suez Canal. The INSTC, a 7,200-kilometer multimodal network, gained significance for Russia after it launched war on Ukraine in 2022.
Currently, 75 percent of the entire project has been completed. From an efficiency standpoint, movement through the INSTC is expected to be 30 percent cheaper and 40 percent shorter than traditional trade routes, such as the Suez Canal. According to the Kazakhstan-based Eurasian Development Bank, the corridor will be able to haul 30 million tons by 2030, providing $1.5 billion in transit fees to Iran.
In addition to this corridor, cargo already moves through St. Petersburg-Astrakhan-Anzali-Bandar Abbas via the Caspian Sea-river link, and through Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan by rail. The next step of the project involves completion of the Rasht-Astara railway, which would give unimpeded railway access from St. Petersburg in Russia to Bandar-Abbas in Iran.

The Horn of Africa countries are among those facing a new security calculus.
Why are the Houthis back in the news?
Andrew Leber: Earlier this month, the Houthis—an armed political movement that has controlled much of Yemen’s territory for more than a decade—claimed control over Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. Their rapid capture of the Port of Mokha marked the group’s first major military advance in nearly five years and shattered a de facto ceasefire brokered by the United Nations. It also further threatened global oil trade at a time when the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has spiked energy prices worldwide.
The Houthis initially stayed out of direct involvement in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which some analysts attributed to the group viewing the battered Islamic Republic as a “weak horse.” Still, their advance into Mokha reflects a steady escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since mid-July, after the collapse of an initial U.S.-Iranian memorandum of understanding. Over the weekend, the Houthis bombed a fuel depot at the main airport in Riyadh, sending a plume of black smoke over the Saudi capital.
This development reflects both the dynamics of a no-longer-frozen domestic Yemeni conflict and continued fallout from the U.S.-Iranian military and diplomatic stalemate in the Persian Gulf. It has also raised the possibility of additional U.S. intervention in the region against the Houthis, though President Donald Trump has thus far declined to use force against the group.
How do these events change the security calculus in the region?
Andrew Leber: The Houthis’ advance gives them control (for now) of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait—a crucial chokepoint at the southern end of the Red Sea. It also raises the possibility of opening a second front in the current Gulf conflict—one that could target Saudi oil facilities and population centers and threaten an additional Red Sea chokepoint for global energy trade and other goods shipments. Past Houthi attacks on Red Sea traffic have already curtailed shipping through the strait while raising insurance and security costs on the remaining vessels.
Previous air campaigns by Saudi Arabia (with the support of other countries) sought to dislodge the Houthis to limit the influence of Iran and Iran-aligned groups on the kingdom’s borders. However, these efforts contributed to a humanitarian catastrophe in Yemen and entrenched the UN-recognized Government of Yemen (GoY) forces in a fraught stalemate with the Houthis. Later military interventions by both the Biden and Trump administrations against Houthi forces likewise ended in strategic defeats.
The latest Houthi advance also calls Saudi Arabia’s bluff that it could contain the Houthis on its own, through a combination of quiet diplomacy and the unification of fragmented GoY forces.
Lesley Anne Warner: In the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Houthis now control the island of Perim (also known as Mayyun), which allows them to more aggressively harass and disrupt maritime traffic. The Houthis’ advance also brings them within 80 miles of Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, which houses Combined Joint Task Force–Horn of Africa and is the United States’ only permanent military facility on the continent. Its mission has previously included operations to support crisis response in the Horn of Africa as well as U.S. combat operations against al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula across the strait in Yemen. Since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas conflict and the resulting impact on maritime insecurity in the Red Sea, Djibouti has reportedly not allowed the United States to use its base for offensive operations against the Houthis. The country has continued to play a balancing act between its criticism of Israel’s approach in Gaza and its utility as a relatively secure, geostrategic country that houses several foreign military bases.
When testifying before Congress last year, General Michael Langley, then the commander of U.S. Africa Command, warned that the Houthis already possessed the capacity to strike the base facilities, should they decide to escalate attacks against the United States or U.S. interests. A recent UN report notes an exchange of weapons and technical training between al-Shabaab—the Somalia-based al-Qaeda affiliate—and the Houthis, with the former providing the latter with hard currency to sustain its political administration and regional military control, and the latter providing the former with advanced weaponry to fight the government in Mogadishu.
With a strengthened Houthi presence in the Bab al-Mandeb, the Houthis and al-Shabaab have more operational space for collaboration. Meanwhile, the Houthis have expanded the battle space and forced any multinational effort to confront them and their Iranian patrons to divide their attention.
These developments come as the United States has been signaling for several years that it will eventually terminate U.S. funding for UN logistical support for the African Union’s stabilization and counter–al-Shabaab mission in Somalia. This development, which would take effect at the end of 2027, is expected to give the militant group more freedom of movement in the areas in which it operates.
How does this affect Saudi Arabia’s energy shipping?
Andrew Leber: Houthi control of Red Sea shipping corridors (at least the southern end) compounds a disastrous period for Saudi energy shipments. Around the same time as the Bab al-Mandeb takeover, Iraq-based militias severely damaged the kingdom’s crucial East-West Pipeline. That energy corridor, combined with Red Sea ports in Jeddah and Yanbu, had allowed Saudi Arabia to offset a significant portion of the U.S.-Iran war’s direct economic costs.
The one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures, however, risks forcing Saudi Arabia into relying more on fraught “dark crossings” of the Strait of Hormuz to evade Iranian attacks—or face a dramatic drop in oil revenues. Tellingly, the kingdom has already begun canceling key oil shipments to Europe.
Houthi gains further complicate efforts by the Arab Gulf states to establish a common position for negotiating with Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia will want some kind of understanding with the Houthis to be part of any Arab-state agreement with Iran, while Iranian leaders will be just as eager to present the Yemen conflict as outside the scope of cross-Gulf relations.
There’s also a Somaliland dimension to this that doesn’t get much attention outside specialist circles. Can you unpack that?
Lesley Anne Warner: Following the 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, and continuing during the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran this year, the Houthis have targeted commercial shipping in the Red Sea—including more recently near the 18-mile-wide Bab al-Mandeb that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The Bab al-Mandeb is a maritime chokepoint through which roughly 12 percent of seaborne-traded oil travels, and the uptick in threats has forced many vessels to reroute around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope. This has increased the strategic value of Somaliland, the partially recognized state that declared independence from Somalia in 1991, and has added to the view in some Washington-based foreign policy circles that the United States should recognize Somaliland’s independence.
The Mogadishu-based federal government has never recognized Somaliland, treating it as an autonomous region. Tensions between Somaliland’s capital, Hargeisa, and Mogadishu escalated in 2024, when Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, granting landlocked Ethiopia a fifty-year lease on approximately 20 kilometers of Somaliland’s coastline for a naval base and commercial port access, with the prospect that the former would extend formal diplomatic recognition to the latter in return. The memorandum provoked fierce opposition from Mogadishu, which accused Addis Ababa of violating its territorial integrity. In December 2024, Türkiye brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia, which committed both parties to respect each other’s territorial integrity and work toward “mutually advantageous” commercial arrangements for Ethiopian port access.
In defense policy circles, increased U.S. military engagement in Somaliland could be perceived as a hedge for the U.S. military presence in Djibouti, where President Ismail Omar Guelleh has been in power for almost three decades and is approaching his eighties. In addition, with the establishment of China’s first overseas military installation in Djibouti in 2017, Djibouti is the only place on the planet that has a permanent military presence from both the United States and China.
Until Israel’s unilateral recognition of the region as an independent state in December 2025, no country had ever recognized Somaliland. There has been speculation as to whether the United States would follow suit, due to Trump’s close relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his frequent disparagement of people of Somali descent as well as Somalia as a whole. In addition, Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi (also known as Irro) was in Washington last week, making the case for Somaliland recognition. WASHINGTON, DC: US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz defended President Donald Trump’s rejection of Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal, calling it a “pretty cynical attempt” to secure concessions.
The proposal would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz and restarted nuclear negotiations in exchange for Washington lifting its naval blockade and easing financial restrictions.
Waltz and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed the rejected plan Sunday, September 27, during separate interviews on NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’.
WELKER: If the president doesn't think this deal is good enough, what deal does he want? What would he accept? 
MIKE WALTZ: Well, I'm not going to negotiate in public for the president
WELKER: But why not give a ceasefire an attempt?
WALTZ: Look, this was I think a pretty… pic.twitter.com/f2mBR598lj
Mike Waltz says Iran sought billions in frozen assets
Waltz argued that Iran’s proposal demanded too much from the United States before negotiations could resume, including access to frozen funds and the lifting of sanctions.
“With this offer came a request to have access to billions in frozen funds, came a request for the lifting of sanctions,” Waltz told host Kristen Welker.
He said the sanctions were international measures, not just American restrictions, and pointed to seven United Nations Security Council resolutions concerning Iran’s nuclear program over the past two decades.
Waltz also cited the International Atomic Energy Agency’s referral of Iran to the Security Council the previous week, saying Tehran had failed to allow appropriate inspections and oversight of its uranium enrichment.
He questioned why Iran needed to enrich uranium to 60%, describing it as a pathway to a nuclear weapon.
He also accused Tehran of pursuing a nuclear program while attacking international shipping.
The ambassador said the administration had little confidence in the latest offer because an earlier memorandum of understanding had been followed by attacks on international shipping, according to his account.
“A pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable,” he said.
He added: “I think it’s kind of common sense that the president doesn’t have a lot of confidence this time.”
Waltz said that Trump would leave all options on the table, while maintaining that the president wanted an arrangement to end the conflict.
Abbas Araghchi challenges Washington over rejected proposal
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi disputed Waltz’s characterization of the proposal in a separate interview on ‘Meet the Press’ and said it offered a practical path toward restoring normal life in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
He argued that the United States had not provided a convincing explanation for rejecting the plan, which required Washington to release frozen Iranian assets, lift its blockade and allow Iran to sell oil.
“Our proposal is very clear. We are ready to open the Strait if certain things are done by the US,” Araghchi said.
The foreign minister accused Washington of repeatedly abandoning negotiations after Iran agreed to engage.
He cited talks in 2025, negotiations in February 2026 and a subsequent agreement that he said the United States violated.
Despite his criticism, Araghchi said he remained willing to negotiate and was waiting for an official response through mediators.
“We are ready to negotiate as much as we are ready to face any challenge,” he said.
Iran’s FM: Iran Is Ready For Diplomacy AND War

He also described the seven-day plan as a way to build confidence before addressing the nuclear dispute in later negotiations.
Iran says it is prepared for renewed fighting amid Trump’s threat
Araghchi said Iran was preparing for the possibility of renewed US military strikes after The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump expected bombing to resume after the November midterm elections.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” he said, adding that Tehran had changed its tactics after previous fighting.
Waltz declined to confirm the report, describing it as anonymous reporting and reiterating that Trump would keep military options available.
The foreign minister also defended Iran’s enrichment of uranium to 60%, arguing that it was legal under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and intended for peaceful purposes.
When Welker asked whether the United States could take the enriched uranium to end the war, Araghchi said Iran had previously offered to address the material during negotiations.
He maintained that diplomacy remained possible, but said Washington would have to demonstrate its willingness to reach an agreement.

The United Arab Emirates and Israel have both confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's unannounced Sunday trip to the Gulf country to meet its president.
President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan hosted Netanyahu in the Emirates Sunday, official media and Netanyahu's office said, in a rare public acknowledgement at a time when the Israeli leader is seen by many as the face of the Gaza genocide.
It appeared to be the first time Abu Dhabi acknowledged a meeting between the duo, confirming earlier Israeli media reports.
Netanyahu's office also confirmed the trip, saying the visit "focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges" amid delicate U.S.-backed diplomacy on the Iran war.
"The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them," the Emirati statement read.
The visit came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the Emirati president had warned Netanyahu ahead of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion, which the Israeli premier did not pass on to the security services.
Netanyahu has denied the story.
According to Israeli media, Netanyahu flew to the UAE Sunday to ask Sheikh Mohamed to deny having given him that warning in 2023.
Earlier Monday, before Netanyahu's office formally confirmed the destination, Israel's domestic security service filed a complaint against a TV channel that reported the visit.
"This evening the Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation," read a statement from Netanyahu's office, which oversees the security agency.
The publication of his visit "endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad" spy agency and other top security officials, the PM's office said in its statement.
The visit was made public when the premier's plane was still outside Israeli airspace, it noted.
Mossad, which also operates under the prime minister's office, issued a similar condemnation, according to the statement.
In May, the UAE had denied reports that Netanyahu secretly visited the country, after Netanyahu's own office said he had met with the UAE president during the war with Iran.
The UAE is a top U.S. ally in the region and one of a handful of Arab nations with official ties to Israel after signing the Abraham Accords during U.S. President Donald Trump's first term in 2020.
The two countries grew closer during the conflict, with Israel reportedly sending its Iron Dome air defense systems, plus personnel to operate them, to the UAE.
